title: Quantifier Order: for all x there exists y versus there exists y for all x
quickIdea: For all x there exists y lets y depend on x. There exists y for all x needs one fixed y that works for every x. The second implies the first, never the reverse.
remember: There exists y for all x R(x, y) implies for all x there exists y R(x, y): valid.
For all x there exists y R(x, y) does not imply there exists y for all x R(x, y): invalid.
Quantifiers of the same kind commute: for all x for all y is the same as for all y for all x, and the same for two existentials.
Mixed quantifiers do not commute; the order is part of the meaning.
Read for all x there exists y as 'choose y after seeing x'; read there exists y for all x as 'one y serves every x'.
Over the integers, for all x there exists y (x < y) is true (take y = x + 1) but there exists y for all x (x < y) is false (no greatest integer).
Negating a nested prefix flips every quantifier and negates the body: not (for all x there exists y R(x, y)) is there exists x for all y not R(x, y).

example.prompt: Over the natural numbers, compare for all x there exists y (y > x) with there exists y for all x (y > x).
example.work: For the first, given any x take y = x + 1. For the second, some single y would have to exceed every natural number, including y itself plus one.
example.answer: The first is true and the second is false.

gateAngle: GATE CS 2023 Q.16 turns on exactly this: option (C), there exists y for all x (P(x) implies Q(x, y)), implies the conjecture for all x (P(x) implies there exists y Q(x, y)), because a single y that works for every x certainly works for each x.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: On the domain {1, 2} with R = {(1, 2), (2, 1)}, which of for all x there exists y R(x, y) and there exists y for all x R(x, y) hold?
variations.answer: The first holds, the second does not.
variations.why: Each x has a partner (1 goes to 2, 2 goes to 1), so every row has a pair. No single y is related to both 1 and 2, so no column is full.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: Does there exists x for all y R(x, y) imply for all y there exists x R(x, y)?
variations.why: If one x is related to every y, then for each y that same x is a witness, so the weaker statement holds.

trap.what: Reading for all x there exists y as though one y had to serve every x.
trap.why: The order decides whether y may depend on x. Swapping a universal and an existential changes the claim from 'a matching column exists' to 'every row has a matching entry'.
trap.counterexample: Domain {1, 2}, R = {(1, 2), (2, 1)}. For all x there exists y R(x, y) is true; there exists y for all x R(x, y) is false.

check.question: Does for all x there exists y R(x, y) imply there exists y for all x R(x, y)? Give the one-line reason.
check.explanation: On {1, 2} with R = {(1, 2), (2, 1)} every row has an entry but no column is full, so the first is true and the second is false.
